demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I acted in ways that go against who I am
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
issues.explanation: The trauma type is accidentally causing serious injury to another person. 'Memory Feels Alien' can occur in PTSD, but paired with the available appraisal pattern it suggests stronger dissociation/self-detachment than is otherwise represented; more importantly, the memory cluster centers on fragmented visual recall and rage, whereas the appraisal cluster centers on guilt/meaning plus personal bodily damage, making the profile feel pulled between different trauma experiences.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: 'Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened' is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type, which is causing serious injury to another person rather than being physically injured oneself. Unless the event also seriously injured the patient, this item is clinically implausible. It also does not fit well with the Memory → Negative Appraisals formulation, because the memory items provided more naturally support guilt, shame, or moral injury appraisals such as 'Violated Values' rather than permanent bodily damage.

vignette:
Harjinder is a 52-year-old South Asian man who works as a hotel housekeeper in a mid-sized city in the Pacific Northwest. He has been divorced for several years and lives alone in a studio apartment not far from the property where he works. He presented for an initial clinical consultation reporting significant distress that has accumulated steadily over the past fourteen months, following an incident at work that he describes, with visible difficulty, as the worst thing he has ever done.

On a morning shift just over a year ago, Harjinder was moving a loaded housekeeping cart along a corridor on the eighth floor of the hotel. He was behind schedule - a circumstance he now returns to obsessively - and had pushed the cart faster than usual around a blind corner near the elevator bank. An elderly guest, a woman in her seventies, was stepping out of the elevator at precisely that moment. The cart struck her with considerable force. She fell, fracturing her hip and sustaining a head laceration that required emergency surgery. Harjinder knelt beside her on the floor while they waited for the paramedics, watching blood collect against the pale carpet. She was conscious but confused, and she looked at him in a way he has never been able to put out of his mind.

The memory of that morning does not come to Harjinder as a continuous narrative. Instead it exists as a sequence of still images - the corner of the cart, the woman's face as she fell, the pattern the blood made, his own hands pressed uselessly against the floor beside her. Each image is vivid and complete in itself, and when one surfaces it carries with it a wave of rage so intense that Harjinder sometimes has to leave whatever room he is in. He is not angry at anyone he could name. The rage seems to have no object except, in his clearer moments, himself.

He had come to believe, with a certainty that no reassurance from his supervisor had touched, that the accident happened because of the way he acted that morning - the rushing, the carelessness, the decision not to slow at the corner. He had worked that job for eleven years and knew the protocol. He had simply chosen not to follow it. This conviction sits at the centre of his inner life now, and it has quietly dismantled the framework of meaning he once had. He used to take a modest but genuine pride in his work, in keeping things orderly and clean, in being reliable. He had thought of himself as a careful man, a man who looked after things. That understanding of himself no longer feels available to him. Nothing in his daily life - his work, his walks, the calls with his adult daughter in Vancouver - carries the weight it once did. He goes through his days as though observing them from a slight distance.

At work, the triggers are everywhere and unavoidable. The elevator bank on the eighth floor is the most potent: on the occasions when his cart must pass it, the full memory can return without any warning, arriving completely and all at once before he has had any chance to prepare himself. The sound of cart wheels on tile has become almost unbearable. He has rearranged his routes where he can, requesting assignments on lower floors, telling his supervisor only that he finds the upper floors difficult. Over the months this has created friction - colleagues have noticed the pattern, his supervisor has grown impatient, and Harjinder has become increasingly isolated from the small social world of the break room, where he once spent his lunch hour. He now eats alone in a stairwell.

What finally brought him to seek help was a conversation with his daughter, who visited in the spring and told him quietly that he seemed to have disappeared. He did not disagree. He came to the clinic not with a clear hope so much as a fear: that the man who caused that woman's injury is now simply who he is, and that nothing that happens in therapy will convince him otherwise.
